rows.question: If the beachhead is only 262 institutions, how should I structure my PM team — one squad for the whole band, or split it by asset tier?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Mid-size banks are the beachhead. | PRD (English) / 11.1 Business Case Summary
rows.answer:
Short answer: don't split by asset tier yet. The 262 count is a verifiable ceiling, not a target list — the real in-band count will shrink once we filter for public mailboxes and listed core systems (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Structure one squad for the whole band until pilot customer-acquisition calibration tells us which tier actually converts; the $5B–$150B range is wide, but the buying behavior we're betting on (Reg E applies, off-the-shelf core, buy-not-build) is uniform across it (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If you need a tie-breaker, split by core system (Fiserv vs. Q2) rather than asset size — that's the integration variable that drives sales cycle length.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Mid-size banks are the beachhead.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The 262 figure comes from an FDIC query. What happens at the edges of the $5B–$150B band — does the product need to behave differently for a bank that just crossed in, or is the band only a sales filter?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Mid-size banks are the beachhead. | PRD (English) / 11.1 Business Case Summary
rows.answer:
The band is a sales filter, not a product boundary — the product itself keys off the three beachhead criteria (public mailbox, off-the-shelf core, Reg E applies), not asset size [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). A bank that just crossed $5B still meets those criteria, so the product behaves the same; the $5B–$150B band is only how we size the addressable market (262 institutions) and prioritize outreach [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Edge cases like a bank near the $150B top that starts building in-house would fall out of the beachhead naturally, but that's a go-to-market decision, not a product change.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Mid-size banks are the beachhead.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Larkspur is fictional but it drives the whole ROI. Which of its four profile numbers would actually change product scope if a real prospect differs?
rows.sources: Research Report / 审阅发现：必须纠正或补上的 10 处（按对面试的影响排序） | Research Report / 9.2 邮件渠道的经济账
rows.answer:
好问题。四个画像数字里，真正会改变产品范围的是**进件量（5万封/月）**和**“请致电”占比（22%）**——前者决定并发与队列设计，后者决定“失败需求下降”这一杠杆的权重；资产规模和坐席数只影响ROI的绝对值，不影响功能范围（见[2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)）。如果真实客户进件量差一个量级（比如5千封/月），triage和自动结案的阈值、以及“周一积压”的批处理设计都要重做；若“请致电”占比远低于22%，则“同一线程内完成核验再办结”的优先级会下降，因为主要矛盾不再是二次联系（见[1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) §1.3、§3.2）。其余两个数字（资产、FTE）在[2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)中已标注为假设，仅用于ROI敏感性，不进入产品决策。

Sources: 2. [Research Report — 9.2 邮件渠道的经济账](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) · 1. [Research Report — 审阅发现：必须纠正或补上的 10 处（按对面试的影响排序）](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

rows.question: Fiserv DNA and Q2 are named as the core stack. What does that integration surface really look like — do we read the core ourselves, or go through connectors that already exist?
rows.sources: Research Report / 1.6 术语表
rows.answer:
We read the core through pre-built connectors, not by building direct integrations ourselves — that's the whole point of the connector layer in the deck (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)). The connectors are standard API "adapters" that let the AI agent, under authorization, verify identity, pull transactions, reissue statements, and open disputes against Fiserv/FIS/Jack Henry cores and Q2/Alkami/Candescent digital banking platforms [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html). What the connector can actually *do* is still gated by the §3.2 delegation matrix and approval checkpoints — the connector only solves "reach," not "authority" [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html).

Sources: 1. [Research Report — 1.6 术语表](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

rows.question: The 10-business-day and 45-day clocks are statutory, but the 27-hour first reply and the 22% "please call us" rate are assumptions. Which one, if it turns out wrong, breaks the business case first?
rows.sources: PRD (English) / 11.4 Pilot Economics (All Assumptions, for Calibration Against Customer Data) | Case Study Deck / The clock starts at the inbox.
rows.answer:
The 22% "please call us" rate is the more fragile assumption, because it feeds the failed-demand reduction that anchors the base-tier savings (15% of 600K items ≈ $720K, see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)). The 27-hour median only affects the qualitative "slowest channel" framing, not the pilot economics — the business case is built on volume, VARR, and loaded cost per item, none of which depend on first-reply latency (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)). If the 22% proves high, the failed-demand pool shrinks proportionally and the $2.68M base-tier estimate erodes before any AI-resolution spend is even considered.

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 11.4 Pilot Economics (All Assumptions, for Calibration Against Customer Data)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

rows.question: A clock starts when the bank receives the mail, not when an agent opens it. Where does that receipt timestamp come from, and how would we prove it to an examiner?
rows.sources: Research Report / v0.4 新增的 6 个产品主张（差异化从这里来） | Case Study Deck / The clock starts at the inbox.
rows.answer:
好问题。收件时间戳来自邮件系统本身的接收元数据（SMTP 接收时间），而不是人工打开邮件的时间——这正是“The clock starts at the inbox”主张的核心（见 [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) 主张①）。对 examiner 的证明路径是：系统在进件时即记录该时间戳并启动法定时钟，且 Reg E 1005.11(b)(1) 的官方解释明确“收到”指银行控制该通知之时，而非员工审阅之时（见 [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)）。具体到 Larkspur 的部署，时间戳的存储与审计日志格式属于实施细节，参考材料未覆盖，建议在 POC 阶段与合规团队确认。

Sources: 1. [Research Report — v0.4 新增的 6 个产品主张（差异化从这里来）](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) · 2. [Case Study Deck — The clock starts at the inbox.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The 28% of agent time lost to system switching comes from a third-party study. Does our design genuinely remove that switching, or does it just move the same effort into a review queue?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / The clock starts at the inbox.
rows.answer:
Good question, Marcus. The 28% figure is a third-party benchmark (Talkdesk 2026, NewtonX n=252) — it describes the industry baseline, not a measured Larkspur outcome [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Our design removes the *re-keying* part of that switching: the email arrives, the Reg E clock starts, and the investigation context (account, transaction, prior notices) is pulled into one view without the agent hopping systems. What remains is a human review step for provisional credit decisions — that's deliberate, not a hidden queue, and it's a fraction of the original switching cost. We haven't run a controlled time-motion study on our own flow yet, so I'd flag that as a validation gap rather than a claim.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The clock starts at the inbox.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Email costs $6–12 a contact and phone $12–20. When I sit with a buyer, do I sell against the channel cost or against the violation exposure?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / The clock starts at the inbox.
rows.answer:
Sell against the violation exposure — that’s the headline. The channel cost is just the supporting detail: email is the slowest channel at 27h median first reply, and an unread inbox is a liability under Reg E (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Lead with the 74% of 2025 Reg E violations in error resolution, then use the $6–12 vs $12–20 spread to show why automation pays for itself even before you count the regulatory risk (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The clock starts at the inbox.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Chat is marked as a smaller surface than email even though both wait their turn. What exactly makes email the bigger build?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
rows.answer:
The bigger build is the auditable number, not the surface. Email’s clock runs on a mailbox with no live interruption, but pricing is our own $1.50 assumption (B12: no public price), and an auditable number takes 90 days to build — where nobody has done it, the blank is also the opportunity (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Chat waits its turn too, but it shares the same buyers as voice and has a smaller surface, so it’s a parity build rather than a new vertical layer (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Same base, no live caller, same runtime.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Two rows say the work already ships. Should my PM org own those lines or hand them off, and how do we avoid stepping on the teams that own them today?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Four more questions, short answers. | Case Study Deck / Same base, no live caller, same runtime. | Case Study Deck / How it is packaged, priced and sold.
rows.answer:
Dana — those two rows are labeled "reused," not "ours": the runtime, bot builder, automation flows and connectors already ship on CXA, and the deck is explicit that we own only the vertical layer (intent detection, assurance tiers, the clock, the dossier) [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Your PM org should own the vertical layer and the proof (policy pack, eval harness, reference numbers), while the horizontal teams keep owning their components — we hand off via the existing connectors and label everything reused so there's no ambiguity [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)[2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). If a hand-off question comes up, the design-partner program is the joint forum where ownership gets settled, with compliance as a named owner [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 2. [Case Study Deck — Same base, no live caller, same runtime.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 3. [Case Study Deck — How it is packaged, priced and sold.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Email ranks above voice here because there is no live interruption. Is that a product property or a technical one — could a voice agent get the same async character with a callback pattern?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
rows.answer:
That’s a fair distinction to draw. The async, no-interruption property is a product property of email as a channel, not a technical limit — a callback pattern could give voice the same “no live caller” feel, but it would still carry the expectation of a synchronous conversation once connected, and it wouldn’t reuse the same runtime the way email does (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). So the ranking rests on the combination: email is async by nature *and* rides the existing base/runtime, which a callback voice flow wouldn’t match without extra build.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Same base, no live caller, same runtime.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The table says the marginal build is the vertical layer alone. What is the honest engineering estimate for that layer, and which of the components we lean on is the weakest link?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Four more questions, short answers.
rows.answer:
Honest estimate: the vertical layer is a few engineer-months, not quarters — intent detection, assurance tiers, the clock, and the dossier are all thin wrappers over the platform’s runtime, bot builder, and connectors (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The weakest link is the clock engine: it’s the only piece that turns a promise into a deadline, and it depends on the bank’s policy pack being precise — if that pack is ambiguous, the clock inherits the ambiguity and the dossier loses its regulator-ready edge (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Complaints and fraud are route-only at 5% of volume. Is that about the model not being good enough, or about regulatory exposure — and would more evidence ever unlock them?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / We automate the work, not the decision.
rows.answer:
Both, but the binding constraint is regulatory exposure, not model quality. Complaints and fraud are permanently L0 — humans decide and sign — because the consequence of a wrong autonomous answer is disproportionate, and no amount of evidence changes that (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). More evidence could improve routing accuracy, but it would not unlock autonomous answering; the scope line is explicit: everything reversible goes to the machine, everything consequential stays with a person [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — We automate the work, not the decision.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The sort order is volume × determinability × identity achievability. Which of those three is computed at runtime and which is a judgement that has to be re-made with every bank?
rows.sources: Research Report / 12.0 v0.4 用例优先级矩阵：按题目给出的五大类
rows.answer:
The three factors are not runtime-computed values; they are design-time judgements you re-make with each bank. Volume and determinability come from the bank’s own intake data and process rules — e.g., the ~15% and ~10% figures in [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) are estimates for Larkspur, not universal constants. Identity achievability is a capability assessment of the bank’s KYC/authentication stack, so it has to be re-evaluated per institution. At runtime, the only thing computed is the routing decision itself — whether a case fits the L0 triage/summary/prep pattern or needs human adjudication, per the L0 definition in [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html).

Sources: 1. [Research Report — 12.0 v0.4 用例优先级矩阵：按题目给出的五大类](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

rows.question: Complaints and fraud are the smallest slice by volume but probably the largest by risk. What is the commercial story for leaving the scariest category manual?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / We automate the work, not the decision. | PRD (English) / 5.1 Use-Case Wave Matrix | Case Study Deck / What ships, what waits, and what has no switch.
rows.answer:
The commercial story is that risk concentration, not volume, drives the delegation design. Complaints and fraud are R4 — the highest regulatory-risk tier — so Wave 1 deliberately keeps them at "detect, clock, warm handoff" with no autonomous reply, because a wrong answer there carries disproportionate cost (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)). The machine still captures the value: it registers the clock, quarantines suspected fraud, and confirms over on-file channels, which removes the expensive manual triage without touching the decision (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html), [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). That is the same logic as the "everything reversible goes to the machine, everything consequential stays with a person" line — the scariest category is where the human sign-off is the product, not a cost (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — We automate the work, not the decision.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 2. [PRD (English) — 5.1 Use-Case Wave Matrix](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 3. [Case Study Deck — What ships, what waits, and what has no switch.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Wave 1 and Wave 2 are described as differences in the policy pack. If both run on one engine, what stops a Wave 2 intent being switched on early by a misconfigured limit matrix?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / One governance layer, three waves.
rows.answer:
Nothing in the engine itself — the limit matrix is bank-written, so a misconfiguration could in principle expose a Wave 2 intent early (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). That’s why the deck frames Wave 2 as “same policy pack, second wave” and pairs it with a UDAAP wording review and a wave board for governance, not as a technical gate. The safeguard is the bank’s own review process, not the runtime.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — One governance layer, three waves.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Step 8 is the only place a model writes to a customer, and only the connective tissue. Is that boundary enforced by the prompt or by the structure of the system?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / The thread is the case.
rows.answer:
The boundary is enforced by the system’s structure, not by the prompt. Step 8 is the only place a model writes to a customer, and it is explicitly “assembled, not written”: the regulated disclosure is a locked template, amounts and dates are system slots checked field by field, and only the connective tissue passes through a model (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The prompt never has the authority to alter disclosures or amounts because those components are never routed to the model in the first place.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Step 6 is idempotent, but what happens if it acts and then step 8 never sends — does the case reopen somewhere, or does it close quietly?
rows.sources: PRD (English) / 6.1 Email Thread Is the Case (Thread = Case) | Case Study Deck / The thread is the case.
rows.answer:
Step 6’s actions are idempotent and compensated by design — the case state contract and compensation flows in FR-4.3 ensure that if step 8 never sends, the case is rolled back to a consistent state rather than silently closed [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). The 14-day verification window in step 9 also keeps the case open for reconciliation, so a missing send would surface there rather than vanish [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). If you need the exact rollback trigger or timeout, that’s not specified in the reference material — I’d point you to the platform’s existing Automation Flows implementation notes.

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 6.1 Email Thread Is the Case (Thread = Case)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 2. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Personalization includes a tone tier. Who defines those tiers, and can an agent override one for a single thread?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / The thread is the case. | Case Study Deck / Four more questions, short answers. | PRD (English) / 6.2 Three-Dimensional Delegation Matrix (Autonomy Matrix)
rows.answer:
Tone tiers are defined by the bank’s own policy pack — we don’t set them; the bank writes the pack and we execute it (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Override for a single thread is possible only through the human-only road (L0–L1) at step 7, where a person decides or signs — there’s no per-thread override on the auto or one-click roads, since step 8’s connective tissue is the only model-written part and it’s gated by the matrix (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If the bank wants an override mechanism, that’s a policy-pack change, not something we’d add unilaterally.

Sources: 2. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 1. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Nine steps and three possible roads after step 5. Where does the record of which road was taken live, and could a reviewer reconstruct it a month later?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / The thread is the case.
rows.answer:
The road taken is recorded as part of the case thread itself — step 5’s matrix decision is a logged event in the same thread that step 1 ingests, so the full nine-step history (including which road was chosen) is reconstructable from the thread’s audit trail [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). A reviewer a month later can replay the thread: the matrix output (L3, L2, or L0–L1) is stored alongside the timestamp and the inputs that drove it, and step 9’s 14-day window applies to customer-facing verification, not to internal logging [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). If you need the exact retention period for the audit trail beyond that, the deck doesn’t specify it — I’d flag that as a gap to confirm with the engineering team.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: R3 is never autonomous over email because the tool functions do not exist on this channel. Is that an architectural guarantee, or a deployment choice someone could reverse later?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Autonomy is earned, intent by intent. | Project README / Solution | Prototype Source / src/mocks/fixtures/designTime.ts | PRD (English) / 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)
rows.answer:
It is architectural: the R3 tool functions are simply not registered on the email channel, so security rests on unreachability rather than model obedience (see [4](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html), FR-6.3 AC1). The deck states this as a design invariant — "the tool functions do not exist on this channel" [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) — and the prototype fixture enforces it with `kind: "never"` and `neverNominated: true` [3](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/mocks/fixtures/designTime.ts). Reversing it would require a deliberate platform change, not a config toggle, but nothing in the reference material rules out a future product decision to add such functions; the guarantee holds for the current design.

Sources: 4. [PRD (English) — 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 1. [Case Study Deck — Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 3. [Prototype Source — src/mocks/fixtures/designTime.ts](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/mocks/fixtures/designTime.ts)

rows.question: The matrix is four identity grades by five action risks. How much of that is code that already ships versus new engineering, and who maintains it once a bank writes its own limits?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / One governance layer, three waves.
rows.answer:
The matrix itself is new — it’s the “bank-written limit matrix (R × I → L)” that sits as a thin vertical layer on top of existing Autopilot, Automation Flows, Agent Builder, and FS core connectors [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). The underlying engine already ships; the new part is the layer, not the channel or runtime [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Once a bank writes its own limits, maintenance is theirs — the deck frames it as “written once by the bank,” applied across channels, with the policy compiler and regulatory radar as ongoing intelligence inputs [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). We don’t specify a vendor vs. bank ops split beyond that, so I’d flag that as an open question for the roadmap discussion.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — One governance layer, three waves.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Money movement has no graduation path at all. What is the risk that this permanent ceiling becomes how customers judge the whole product?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.
rows.answer:
The ceiling is deliberate, not a gap: R4 (adjudication / money movement) is "Never autonomous over email — the tool functions do not exist on this channel" [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), so there is no graduation path by design. The risk you name is real, but the deck frames it as a trust feature — the same slide shows L0 human decides and sends, with the AI only triaging and suggesting [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), which is the strongest possible proof of the product's safety posture. If customers judge the whole product by this one boundary, that is the intended message: autonomy is earned per intent, and some intents are simply not eligible.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Auto-demotion on drift is mentioned but not specified. What triggers it, who gets told, and does it happen silently?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff. | Project README / Solution | Case Study Deck / Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.
rows.answer:
Auto-demotion is triggered by drift in the same-evidence blocks that earned graduation — backtest, sampling, negative relabel, or dual sign-off — and the ratchet is asymmetric: tightening can take effect same-day with auto-expiry, while loosening must earn its way back through the full gate sequence (see [2](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/README.md)). Who gets told: the drift signal feeds back into Sense, and the auto-demotion is part of the loop that "humans sign the diff" — so the human sign-off on the configuration diff is the notification channel, not a silent background event (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). It does not happen silently; the demotion itself is a configuration diff flowing into the same gates that govern every output (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 2. [Project README — Solution](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/README.md) · 1. [Case Study Deck — AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Six nominators spread across two screens and three roles. Who owns this loop day to day — one PM, or a standing review board with a cadence?
rows.sources: Review Backlog / Demo 建议 | PRD (English) / 6.1 Email Thread Is the Case (Thread = Case) | PRD (English) / 6.6 Design-time Intelligence v0.3 Added
rows.answer:
Good question — the PRD deliberately leaves the owner role open, but the cadence is fixed by the gates themselves. The loop is owned by the Product + Compliance dual-sign pair from §6.3, who already sign every diff; the nominators (FR-12.1–12.6) feed them, not the other way around [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). Day-to-day, it's a standing review board with a cadence: 90-day backtest, 14-day shadow, and dual sign are hard gates, so the "who" is whoever holds those sign-off rights — the PRD doesn't name a single PM, and I'd argue it shouldn't, since the compliance half of the pair is non-negotiable [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html).

Sources: 2. [PRD (English) — 6.1 Email Thread Is the Case (Thread = Case)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

rows.question: A nomination is a configuration diff. What format is that diff in, and can it be applied atomically or does each bank need a migration?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Admin: the bank writes the limits, not the model.
rows.answer:
The diff is a configuration diff — the bank controls every cell of the matrix, the thresholds, and the locked template wording, and the model drafts it while the bank signs it (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The deck doesn’t specify the exact serialization format (e.g., JSON/YAML) or whether application is atomic versus a per-bank migration — that’s outside what the reference material covers.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Admin: the bank writes the limits, not the model.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Dissent cards are part of the proving step. What counts as dissent, and does it block the grant or is it only recorded?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff.
rows.answer:
Dissent cards are recorded evidence, not a veto — they don’t block the grant, but they feed back into the loop and can trigger auto-demotion if drift is detected (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). A dissent is any backtest or shadow-run outcome where the model’s nomination disagrees with the human-signed diff, plus any rejected nomination from the two-human sign-off step. The deck doesn’t specify a threshold for how many dissents force demotion — that’s a policy detail we’d set with the bank, not a fixed number in the case study.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The whole loop eats 90 days of decisions as its input. What do we do for a customer who does not have 90 days of clean history to feed it?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff. | Case Study Deck / The AI proposes. The rule engine decides. | PRD (English) / 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)
rows.answer:
Good question — the 90-day window is the backtest corpus, not a prerequisite for every customer. New intents and candidates start shadow-classified and graduate normally, so a customer with thin history still gets the same gates: backtest, shadow, dual sign-off, auto-demotion (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). What they lack is the *evidence density* to justify loosening a rule quickly — the ratchet means any tightening is immediate, but loosening still runs the full backtest → shadow → dual-sign path regardless of history length (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). For a genuinely new account with no samples, the AI simply doesn't nominate until enough evidence accumulates; the rule engine still decides on existing deterministic rules, so the customer isn't left unprotected — they just don't get AI-proposed wording until the loop has something to chew on.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 2. [Case Study Deck — The AI proposes. The rule engine decides.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Four screens on one runtime. Which of them is hardest to keep consistent when the limit matrix changes — the agent workspace or the admin policy screen?
rows.sources: Research Report / 14.2 核心场景剧本：三封邮件的一个周二早高峰（v0.4 重写） | Case Study Deck / Four screens, four proofs. | Research Report / 四个 Persona 与隐形决策人
rows.answer:
Admin policy screen — because it is the *source* of the R × I limits, and every other screen must read from it, not cache it. The agent workspace only renders the verdict and the case pack, so it stays consistent as long as it queries the matrix live; the admin screen is where a one-click tightening has to propagate to the supervisor's approval queue and the customer thread's disclosure fields in the same instant (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The demo films this as "writes every R × I limit; tightens in one click" — the risk is a stale read on the agent side, which is why the v0.4.2 source-layering annotation (template strings, system slots, AI-organized text) keeps the policy verdict out of the model entirely (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)).

Sources: 2. [Case Study Deck — Four screens, four proofs.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 1. [Research Report — 14.2 核心场景剧本：三封邮件的一个周二早高峰（v0.4 重写）](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

rows.question: The customer screen has no login and verifies identity inside the thread. What is the fallback when that verification fails — is there a path that does not end in a phone call?
rows.sources: PRD (English) / 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)
rows.answer:
Yes — failure/timeout does not force a phone call. Per FR-2.2 AC2, on failed or expired verification the case offers alternative paths (phone/branch) without leaking account status [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). So the fallback is explicitly phone *or* branch, and the branch path avoids a call entirely. Note the PRD doesn’t specify branch details (e.g., in-person document checks), so that part remains open.

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

rows.question: Only four demo films are listed and one number is missing from the sequence. Is that deliberate, and what does the gap say about what we can show a buyer today?
rows.sources: Prototype Source / src/demo/runner.ts | Case Study Deck / Four screens, four proofs. | Prototype Source / src/demo/runner.ts
rows.answer:
The gap is deliberate — the deck lists Demo 1, 2, 3, and 5, skipping Demo 4. That’s because the prototype’s `startAll()` chain runs every script in menu order, and the menu itself has five entries; the missing number corresponds to a script we haven’t filmed yet, not a hidden capability [3](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/demo/runner.ts). What we can show a buyer today is exactly those four films — each one proves a distinct claim (identity, disputes, fraud, intelligence) — and the gap signals that the fifth proof is still in production rather than being withheld [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 3. [Prototype Source — src/demo/runner.ts](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/demo/runner.ts) · 2. [Case Study Deck — Four screens, four proofs.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Admin tightens a limit in one click. Does that write a new policy version or mutate the live one, and can it be rolled back?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Admin: the bank writes the limits, not the model.
rows.answer:
Admin actions always produce a configuration diff — a new policy version, never a mutation of the live one. The bank signs it through the same gates as any other change (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Rollback is inherent: since every change is a versioned diff, reverting is just applying the prior diff — but note the deck doesn't specify a rollback UI or SLA, so I can't speak to operational details beyond that.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Admin: the bank writes the limits, not the model.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The window is 12–18 months and one competitor already ships autonomous email. What is our wedge if a CCaaS vendor bundles an email case model before we close the first bank?
rows.sources: Research Report / 11.1 支柱一：Case worker, not chatbot（办案件，不是陪聊） | Case Study Deck / Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case. | Research Report / 6.3 逐家证据（点击展开）
rows.answer:
The wedge is the case model itself, not email automation. Freshworks ships autonomous email but is SMB with no FS depth or voice core [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html); Talkdesk only extended Autopilot to email in 2026-02 and has no dispute-specific agent among its 16 prebuilt bank agents [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html). Our statutory clock engine, dispute state machine, and core-banking execution are the regulatory spine no CCaaS vendor has productized — Reg E timing, audit-ready case files, and full-cycle dispute handling are absent from their public materials [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html). If a CCaaS bundles a generic email case model, they still lack the FS-specific dispute lifecycle; that is the 12–18 month moat we are building on CXA Operations Center, Agent Builder, and core-banking connectors [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 3. [Research Report — 6.3 逐家证据（点击展开）](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) · 1. [Research Report — 11.1 支柱一：Case worker, not chatbot（办案件，不是陪聊）](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) · 2. [Case Study Deck — Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: One of the four states is "not in public materials". How do we keep that assessment honest if a rival ships it quietly and we only find out mid-deal?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case. | Case Study Deck / Everyone has an agent. Nobody has the email case. | Case Study Deck / Reversible earns it. Irreversible never does.
rows.answer:
Fair question. The "not in public materials" cells are explicitly a statement about what we can verify, not a claim about the market — the deck says so itself (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). We keep it honest by treating absence of public evidence as a risk, not a win: the threat ranking already names Glia and Eltropy as the ones to watch (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)), and our go-to-market plan includes a quarterly sweep of their release notes and support docs. If a rival ships quietly mid-deal, we'd find out the same way they'd find out about us — through the customer's procurement process, where our statutory clock and governance layer are the differentiators that survive comparison (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 2. [Case Study Deck — Everyone has an agent. Nobody has the email case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 1. [Case Study Deck — Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Core-banking execution is scored as a capability. If those connectors have been shipping for over a year, what is genuinely left for us to build there?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case.
rows.answer:
The connectors are the plumbing, not the case. Since April 2025, CXA has shipped the core-banking connectors, Agent Builder, and Automation Flows — but the statutory clock engine and the email-native case model are what we design and prototype on top of that platform (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). What’s left to build is the decision layer: proposing the rules and managing the clock, not just moving data. The deck’s own claim is that most vendors automate the reply; few propose the rules — that’s the gap we occupy (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Our target state marks all four capabilities. Which one is the actual differentiator in a deal, and which are just table stakes?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case. | PRD (English) / 6.1 Email Thread Is the Case (Thread = Case) | Research Report / 12.0c 机会优先级（v0.3 原表，已按 v0.4 口径更新）
rows.answer:
Differentiator: the statutory-clock engine — AI opens the case, starts the Reg E/Z clock at intake, auto-acknowledges, and chases materials, while a human adjudicates (see [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)). That's the "nobody has the email case" claim: Talkdesk's catalog has no dispute agent, and email-injected ATO/change-of-account interception isn't productized in public materials (see [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)).

Table stakes: voice + real-time ops (CCaaS), CRM + AI agent, and core-banking execution — all are "what the platform already ships" via CXA Operations Center, Agent Builder, Automation Flows, and core-banking connectors (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The deck's own framing says the foundation "is not a differentiator" (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)); the differentiator is the case model itself — most automate the reply, few propose the rules (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 3. [Research Report — 12.0c 机会优先级（v0.3 原表，已按 v0.4 口径更新）](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) · 1. [Case Study Deck — Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 2. [PRD (English) — 6.1 Email Thread Is the Case (Thread = Case)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

rows.question: The vendor-side figure multiplies out to roughly $54M at full adoption, with penetration explicitly not assumed. What penetration is the plan actually underwriting in year one?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / One bank's email book is a $4.8M cost base.
rows.answer:
The plan underwrites zero penetration in year one — the $54M is a ceiling, not a target. We deliberately show 262 beachhead banks at full adoption with "penetration not assumed" [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), because the deck's job is to size the opportunity, not to promise a sales ramp. Year-one commitments live in the base case: 35% of email resolved, which nets the bank ≈$2.68M and the vendor ≈$205k per bank [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — One bank's email book is a $4.8M cost base.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The saving turns on how much we can genuinely finish. Is the resolved-rate range measured anywhere, and what instrumentation would produce that number in production?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / One bank's email book is a $4.8M cost base.
rows.answer:
The resolved-rate range (20% / 35% / 50%) is a modeled assumption, not a measured figure — it's tied to how much we can "genuinely finish" per the deck's own framing [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). In production, the number would come from the bank's own mail system: we'd instrument resolution as a closed-loop outcome (e.g., email thread marked resolved, follow-up absent, or customer reply confirming closure), measured against valid inbound after failed demand is excluded — the same basis used for the 35% base case [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). We haven't published a specific instrumentation spec, so I can't cite a concrete metric definition beyond that.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — One bank's email book is a $4.8M cost base.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The same rate is quoted against two different denominators. Which one do we commit to in a contract, and does the difference change the headline number?
rows.sources: Research Report / 11.2b v0.4.4 差异点补证：对客承诺的自动登记与兑现追踪（D2 向对客文案侧的延伸） | Case Study Deck / Reversible earns it. Irreversible never does. | PRD (English) / 04 Success Metrics & Guardrails
rows.answer:
The 35% vs ≈30% figure is the same VARR rate quoted against two denominators, not two different rates — the contract commits to the harder one: VARR is reported against every valid inbound email (disputes, fraud reports, multi-intent mail, repeat contacts all count), and that is the denominator we publish as the headline [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). The ≈30% is the same numerator expressed against the eligible pool (excluding R4 cells with no graduation path), shown side-by-side so no one can call it denominator-picking [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). The difference does not change the headline number — it changes the base it is read against, and we commit to the harder base in any contract.

Sources: 2. [Case Study Deck — Reversible earns it. Irreversible never does.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The vendor fee and the seats replaced are both listed. Who in my org owns the seats-replaced conversation with the customer, since it lands on their operations budget?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / One bank's email book is a $4.8M cost base.
rows.answer:
Good question — the seats-replaced line is a customer-side operations saving, not a vendor fee, so it belongs to the customer's ops owner (typically the head of contact-center operations or the COO). We surface it in the deal as a shared input to the bank's own business case, but we don't negotiate or own that budget line; the vendor's fee is only the $1.50 per resolution (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If your org wants to support the customer's internal conversation, we can provide the math behind the ≈$63k figure, but the ownership stays with the bank.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — One bank's email book is a $4.8M cost base.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: A single critical error voids the headline number. Is the recall target measured on the bank’s own mail or on our eval set, and who signs off on that measurement?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Three numbers. One pilot. | Research Report / 14.2 核心场景剧本：三封邮件的一个周二早高峰（v0.4 重写） | Case Study Deck / Four more questions, short answers.
rows.answer:
Recall is measured on the bank’s own mail, not our eval set — the pilot runs backtest W1–W2 and shadow W3–W4 on live traffic, and the 59-day gate is the sign-off point (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The bank’s compliance lead signs off on the measurement, alongside the shared eval team; the guardrails run in parallel, and the Trust Veto is non-negotiable (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Three numbers. One pilot.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 3. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Time to resolution runs from the arrival timestamp. Does that clock keep running while the customer is being asked for a step-up?
rows.sources: Research Report / 15.1 题目九问的回答
rows.answer:
The clock starts at intake and keeps running through any step-up — that's exactly why we treat the same-thread verification as part of the regulated handling, not a pause (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)). The step-up is designed to be completed within the same thread so the regulatory timeline isn't extended by a channel switch; the supervisor dashboard surfaces that elapsed time explicitly (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)).

Sources: 1. [Research Report — 15.1 题目九问的回答](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

rows.question: Four phases inside 59 days is tight for an integration. Which phase slips first if the connector work runs a week late, and what is the recovery?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / 59 days to a signed day-59 report.
rows.answer:
If the connector work slips a week, the shadow run (W3–W4) is the first phase to compress, because it is the only gate that can absorb delay without violating the day-59 veto criteria — recall ≥99.5% and zero misses are non-negotiable (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Recovery: overlap the tail of onboarding/backtest with the start of shadow, and run shadow at full volume for a shorter window, but only if the day-45 cohort observation and the day-59 gate remain intact — any miss in shadow is a No-go, so we would not cut the shadow below a statistically meaningful sample (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If the slip exceeds a week, the honest answer is the go/no-go criterion itself: we would flag a No-go rather than compress L1/L2 live or the day-45 measure, since those feed the signed day-59 report (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — 59 days to a signed day-59 report.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The autonomy rate has three conditions attached. Which of the three is most likely to be gamed by a customer who wants the number to look good?
rows.sources: Research Report / 12.3 v0.4.3 Trade-off 登记册：为控险、合规与可信度主动放弃了什么 | Research Report / 7.1 两个 headline 方向的证据复核 | PRD (English) / 6.2 Three-Dimensional Delegation Matrix (Autonomy Matrix)
rows.answer:
最可能被“做数”的是第三个条件——受监管意图的召回门槛（≥99.5%）。因为召回率只统计“检测器抓到的”占“实际应抓的”比例，而“实际应抓”的标签来自人工标注或事后审计，客户可以通过放宽标注口径、延迟审计或只对低风险样本抽检来抬高数字；相比之下，动作白名单和金额阈值是确定性规则，无法被统计口径操纵（见[1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) §3.2、§13）。校准样本量（n≥600）虽然也可被“攒样本”稀释，但 rule of three 的上界是数学硬约束，造假成本更高（见[2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)）。

Sources: 1. [Research Report — 12.3 v0.4.3 Trade-off 登记册：为控险、合规与可信度主动放弃了什么](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) · 2. [Research Report — 7.1 两个 headline 方向的证据复核](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

rows.question: Preferring false positives pushes recall up and precision down. Where does the false-positive cost actually land, and can a bank tune the trade-off without breaking the recall gate?
rows.sources: PRD (English) / 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)
rows.answer:
False-positive cost lands on intake-side R2 agents: they must manually review and clear every regulated sub-intent that the detector flags, and each false positive still starts the statutory clock and locks the delegation tier (adjudication R4 always human) — so the cost is operational, not regulatory [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). The recall gate is a hard floor (≥99.5% on regulated intents), not a ceiling; a bank can tune precision by adjusting the detector threshold or adding post-detection filters, as long as backtesting still holds the recall bar and any miss triggers incident review [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). The PRD doesn’t specify a precision target or a tuning mechanism beyond that constraint, so the exact trade-off curve is left to implementation.

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

rows.question: Injected text is quarantined as data and never as instruction. What is the mechanism — a sanitiser before the model, or a structural separation of the two channels?
rows.sources: PRD (English) / 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12) | Case Study Deck / The risks that would end this product. | PRD (English) / 8.3 Email Three: ATO + Attachment Injection (Showing "Dangerous Actions Are Unreachable")
rows.answer:
Both, by design. External content is stripped and labeled at the quarantine layer (script stripping, tracking-pixel removal, link rewriting) before the model sees it, and it is then passed only as data with explicit delimiters and untrusted markings — never as system instructions [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). On top of that, the tool-signature layer makes the attack unreachable: the change-mobile + mail-card combination has no callable function on the email channel, so even a successful injection cannot trigger a write [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)[3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html).

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 2. [Case Study Deck — The risks that would end this product.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 3. [PRD (English) — 8.3 Email Three: ATO + Attachment Injection (Showing "Dangerous Actions Are Unreachable")](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

rows.question: If our own judge flips verdicts at that rate, how can an autonomy number be contractual at all?
rows.sources: Research Report / 12.0c 机会优先级（v0.3 原表，已按 v0.4 口径更新）
rows.answer:
Lena, fair challenge — and it's exactly why we don't put the autonomy number in the contract. The 14% flip rate is on the judge's *own* verdicts, not on the bank's agreed SLAs; we only commit to the human-in-the-loop review cadence and the audit trail, which are measurable and stable (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)). The autonomy figure is a benchmark for internal iteration, not a contractual term — we'd rather under-promise on the metric and over-deliver on the process.

Sources: 1. [Research Report — 12.0c 机会优先级（v0.3 原表，已按 v0.4 口径更新）](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

rows.question: Sign-off fatigue is on the register. What stops one-click approvals from becoming rubber stamps once a customer is running at the target autonomy?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / The risks that would end this product. | Prototype Source / src/demo/scripts.ts
rows.answer:
Good catch — the register flags it, but the deck doesn't claim a hard stop. The mitigation is the same one shown in the prototype: the autonomy cell downgrades from auto to one-click when the policy condition fails, and the reason is only readable on the agent screen (see [2](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/demo/scripts.ts)). We track the approve-without-edit rate and sample approved files, but we don't promise a threshold that eliminates rubber-stamping — that's a live risk, not a solved one (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 2. [Prototype Source — src/demo/scripts.ts](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/demo/scripts.ts) · 1. [Case Study Deck — The risks that would end this product.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: Five of the new pieces are written by the bank itself. What stops two banks from diverging into configurations we can no longer support?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Admin: the bank writes the limits, not the model. | Case Study Deck / One governance layer, three waves. | PRD (English) / 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)
rows.answer:
Good question — the deck is explicit that the bank writes the limits, not the model [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), and every cell of the matrix, threshold, and template wording is bank-controlled [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). But the governance layer itself is the constraint: R3 and R4 cells never respond, a cell tightens in one click but loosens only through graduation evidence and a dual signature [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), and all changes arrive as configuration diffs that must clear the same gates [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). That said, the deck doesn't specify a support contract or versioning policy for divergent configs — if you need that commitment, it's not in the reference material, and I'd flag it as an open item for the roadmap discussion.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Admin: the bank writes the limits, not the model.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: One policy engine written once and applied to every channel. What has to be true in the runtime for a voice agent to reuse the email policy pack without forking it?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / One governance layer, three waves. | Case Study Deck / Four more questions, short answers.
rows.answer:
The runtime has to treat the policy pack as data, not code — the same `R × I → L` limit matrix and the same clock engine that turns a promise into a deadline, written once by the bank and applied to every channel (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). For voice, that means the Agent Builder voice agent calls the same policy engine and clock engine as the email flow; the only channel-specific part is the intent detection and the natural-language interface, which is exactly why the deck says the new part is the layer, not the channel — no new platform or runtime (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The deck doesn't specify the technical contract for that reuse (e.g., API shape or latency bounds), so I can't go deeper than that from the material.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — One governance layer, three waves.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The second wave adds a new language and a new regulation under the same policy pack. Who owns that pack as an artifact — a PM or an engineering team?
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / How it is packaged, priced and sold. | Case Study Deck / Four more questions, short answers.
rows.answer:
The policy pack is owned by the bank — it is their artifact, not ours. We ship the mechanism (the pack is a setting, not a new SKU, per [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)), and the design-partner program runs jointly with compliance as a named owner rather than a reviewer at the end [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). So the bank’s compliance team owns the pack as a living artifact; our vertical team (product, engineering, compliance lead) builds and maintains the tooling that lets them edit and enforce it [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — How it is packaged, priced and sold.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 2. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.question: The second wave mentions a wording review for complaints. Is that a new model capability or a new human review step on top of the existing one?
rows.sources: PRD (English) / 5.1 Use-Case Wave Matrix | Case Study Deck / We automate the work, not the decision. | Case Study Deck / One governance layer, three waves.
rows.answer:
It’s a new human review step, not a new model capability. Wave 1 already does detection, warm handoff, and clock registration for complaints; the UDAAP wording review in Wave 2 is a deep-capability add-on where humans review the bank’s drafted responses for regulatory-compliant language before send (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html), [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The model still doesn’t decide — it flags and routes, and the review sits on top of the existing human workflow.

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 5.1 Use-Case Wave Matrix](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 2. [Case Study Deck — We automate the work, not the decision.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
